name: Breast cancer & lumps
tagline: Self-check, screening, and what to do if you find a lump.

urgent.heading: See a clinic this week if
urgent.primary_message: A new breast lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or shape changes — do not wait. Get it checked. Most are not cancer, but the ones that are need fast action.
red_flags: A new lump or thickening in the breast or armpit
Change in size, shape, or symmetry of one breast
Skin dimpling, puckering, or orange-peel texture
Nipple turning inward, or new discharge (especially bloody)
Persistent skin redness, scaling, or rash on the nipple
Persistent pain in one specific spot
Swollen lymph nodes in the armpit or above the collarbone

what_is_it.heading: Breast cancer in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Breast cancer is cancer that starts in the cells of the breast — usually in the milk ducts or the milk-producing glands. Most breast lumps are not cancer, but every new lump needs to be checked.
paragraphs: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in South African women. About 1 in 27 will develop it in their lifetime. Men can get breast cancer too, though it is much rarer — about 1 in 1,000.

When caught early — before it spreads — breast cancer is highly treatable. Five-year survival for early stage breast cancer in SA is over 80%. The challenge in South Africa is late detection: many women only see a doctor once the cancer is advanced, when treatment is harder and outcomes are worse.

items.headline: 1 in 27
items.body: South African women will develop breast cancer in their lifetime. The risk rises sharply after age 50.

items.headline: Most lumps benign
items.body: Around 8 out of 10 breast lumps are not cancer — cysts, fibroadenomas, or normal breast changes. But every new lump still needs assessment.

items.headline: Early = survival
items.body: Five-year survival is over 80% when caught early, dropping sharply if found late. Early detection is the single biggest factor in outcome.

items.headline: Free screening
items.body: Free clinical breast exams at every clinic. Mammograms free at state hospitals for women over 40 with risk factors. CANSA mobile screening too.

pull_quote.text: Most breast lumps are not cancer. But you cannot tell by feel alone. Every new lump that does not go away in one menstrual cycle deserves a clinic visit. Do not 'wait and see' for months.

signs.heading: What to look for
signs.lede: Get to know what your breasts normally look and feel like. Changes from your normal are what matter — not how your breasts compare to someone else's.

items.title: Lumps and thickening
items.description: A new lump in the breast or armpit. An area that feels different — firmer, denser, or thicker than the surrounding tissue. Most are not cancer but all need to be checked.

items.title: Changes in shape or skin
items.description: One breast looking different from before — size, shape, or position changing. Dimpling, puckering, or orange-peel skin. Persistent redness or rash.

items.title: Nipple changes
items.description: Nipple turning inward (newly), discharge that is not breast milk (especially bloody or clear from one side), or a scaly rash on the nipple.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Breast cancer only happens to older women.
items.fact: Risk rises sharply after 50, but breast cancer happens at any age. Younger women's cancer tends to be more aggressive — every age group needs to know the signs.

items.myth: If no one in my family has had breast cancer, I am safe.
items.fact: Only about 1 in 10 breast cancers are clearly linked to inherited genes. Most happen to women with no family history. Everyone needs to know the signs.

items.myth: Wearing a bra or using deodorant causes breast cancer.
items.fact: Neither has been shown to cause breast cancer in any reliable study. These are myths that distract from the things that actually matter — early detection and known risk factors.

items.myth: A small lump is nothing to worry about.
items.fact: Size does not tell you whether a lump is cancer. Some aggressive cancers are tiny when found; most large lumps are not cancer. Get any new lump checked — regardless of size.

prevention.heading: How to lower the risk and catch it early
prevention.lede: Some risk factors you cannot change (age, genes, sex). Many you can. Early detection is the strongest predictor of survival.

items.title: Know your normal
items.description: Look at and feel your breasts once a month, ideally after your period. Changes from your normal are what matter — get familiar with what 'normal' is for you.

items.title: Clinical exam at clinic
items.description: Free clinical breast exam at any government clinic — annually from age 30. Health workers find things you might miss.

items.title: Mammogram from 40
items.description: Mammograms are recommended every 2 years from age 40, yearly if higher risk. State hospitals offer free mammograms for women at risk.

items.title: Lifestyle factors
items.description: Maintain a healthy weight, limit alcohol (under 1 drink a day), be physically active, breastfeed if you can. These reduce risk modestly but meaningfully.

items.title: If you find a new lump
items.description: Note when you found it. See a clinic within the next two weeks. If you are nearing or past menopause, do not wait through any 'cycle' — see someone sooner.

items.title: Do a monthly self-check
items.description: Once a month, after your period. Look in the mirror with arms raised. Feel each breast and armpit in circular motions. Standing and lying down. Five minutes.

items.title: Annual clinical exam from 30
items.description: Walk into any clinic. Ask for a clinical breast exam. Free, takes minutes, and finds things you cannot feel yourself.

items.title: Mammogram from age 40
items.description: Every 2 years from 40, yearly if at higher risk (family history, dense breasts, BRCA gene). Discomforting but quick — and life-saving.

items.title: If diagnosed — get to a cancer centre
items.description: Treatment is most effective at major hospital cancer centres. Ask about referral. CANSA can help navigate the system.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Breast cancer care in South Africa is well-organised at the major centres. The earlier in the system you enter, the better the outcomes.
